name: Lettie Burchett
languages: Enough Italian and Hungarian to deliver a baby in either
equipment: Heavy coat: a brown wool coat her husband bought her in 1915 from a Sears catalogue, mended at both elbows
Kitchen knife, a good butcher's knife with a beech handle, which goes in her bag because a midwife needs a clean blade
Midwife's bag: clean sheets, scissors, cord tape, carbolic soap, a bottle of whiskey, a tin of lard, a pair of scales and a little brass bell for the mothers to ring
A nurse's pin from her two years' training at a Charleston hospital, 1889 to 1891
A watch pinned to her dress, which belonged to her husband Wash
A company scrip slip, $50, 'special work, 7 North, 18 Oct 1919', in Wash's name, never spent, folded in her Bible
A family Bible with three generations of births written in the front, a good half of them babies she caught herself
A paper of salt, a candle stub and matches in her apron pocket, because her grandmother always carried them
features: Something to Hold On To (Faithful origin: once per long rest, when she would gain Dread, she gains 1 fewer; advantage on saves against being charmed or compelled by a creature; no miracle in it, only staying herself)

The Thin Place (Sensitive: she knows when a presence is within 60 ft, though not where or what; feels cold spots and wrongness before anyone else, and the GM tells her the strongest emotion soaked into any room she enters; once per scene she opens herself to the place and the GM gives her one true impression, at the cost of 1 Dread, no save; never control, never magic)
Read the Room (Sensitive: advantage on Insight checks to tell what a person is feeling, and she knows without a check when someone she speaks with is frightened, grieving or hiding something)

Closer to the Edge (Sensitive, 2nd level: Dread from The Thin Place can't take her past Dread 5; at Dread 3 or more, The Thin Place gives two impressions, and she can tell where a presence is to within 10 ft)
Gift: Listener (Sensitive, 3rd level: her impressions often come as voices; once per scene she can hear the last words spoken in a place where someone died, as the GM chooses to give them)

On the Ward (Nurse background: doctors, nurses and every mother in the camp treat her as one of their own; she can get into any sickroom, read a chart without a check, and people tell her what they would not tell a preacher)

personality.traits: I talk to everybody like I've known them since they were born, which mostly I have. I say grace before I eat and before I go down a cellar. I can be quiet for an hour and it is never awkward, for me.
personality.ideals: Everybody comes into the world the same way and every one of them is worth the trouble. I have caught three hundred and eleven babies in this hollow, Black and white and foreign, and I did not ask any of them what their daddy thought about the union.
personality.bonds: My husband Wash, dead three years, who told me the truth the night he died and asked me to keep it. The camp, every house of it. Mavis Shumate, whom I caught in 1893 and who is the nearest thing I have to a daughter.
personality.flaws: I have kept Wash's secret for three years because I was afraid of what it would do to the men who were on that crew with him, and to me. I hear things in the ground, and I have got used to not telling anyone, and some of what I hear I should have told.

appearance: A small, round, strong-armed woman of fifty-seven with iron-grey hair in a knot, a brown weathered face, very dark eyes, and hands that have never once been cold to a patient. A brown coat, an apron, sturdy shoes, a black bag, and a habit of tilting her head as if she were listening to something under the floor.
backstory: Lettie Burchett was born Lettie Sowards on a hill farm on Shumate Ridge in 1870, long before there was a mine or a town, learned midwifery from her grandmother, and went down to Charleston at nineteen to train two years as a nurse because her grandmother said the new ways were worth knowing too. She married Washington Burchett, a coal loader, in 1902, when Ottway was a new camp of raw board houses, and has been the hollow's granny woman ever since: she catches the babies, sits with the dying, sets the bones old Dr. Whitlock could not be bothered with, and knows every family in all five rows of the camp. She has always heard things other people do not, a cold in a room, a voice in an empty house, and she was raised to think that was nothing to be ashamed of and nothing to talk about. Wash was on the seal crew in October 1919. He came home every night for two days and would not eat, and on the third day he got a fifty-dollar scrip slip for 'special work' and put it in her Bible and never touched it. He testified at the inquest and did not answer the one question that mattered. In 1924 a slate fall broke his back in 5 South, and on the last night, with the lamp low, he told her: 'We heard them, Lettie. Fourteen of them, knocking on the rail. Bledsoe said it was the mountain. We kept on laying block. Then they capped the air shaft on Shumate's, and the knocking went on six more days, and then it quit.' Since the first of March she has been hearing knocking again, at night, under her kitchen floor, four and then two. Her house is the last on Number Two Bottom, nearest the drift mouth.
